Bay anchovy Anchoa mitchilli is a small, short-lived clupeiform fish that dominates the ichthyoplankton of many estuarine systems along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of North America. Spawning occurs primarily during the warm summer months when water temperatures are elevated, with individual females releasing multiple batches of fertilised ova over an extended breeding season. The fertilised eggs are transparent, pelagic, and measure approximately 0.8 mm in diameter, a size that directly influences the mass of the newly emerged prolarva. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva carries an endowment of endogenous yolk that sustains it during the first days of life. Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the interval from fertilisation to rupture of the chorion is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a duration that aligns well with the rapid developmental rates characteristic of small-bodied marine teleosts. The resulting yolk-sac larva has a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.00027 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.00027 grams], reflecting the modest amount of yolk packaged into the egg by the female prior to spawning. This tiny mass represents the starting point for a growth trajectory that, under optimal thermal and feeding regimes, leads to dramatic size increases over the ensuing weeks and months.

As the prolarva depletes its yolk reserves and transitions to exogenous feeding, the onset of first feeding marks a critical bottleneck in early survival. The mouth of the larva opens and retinal differentiation enables prey detection, allowing the now exogenously feeding larva to capture small copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. Growth during the pelagic larval stage is rapid, and individuals undergo a larval-juvenile transition involving fin ray ossification and scale formation as they approach the metamorphic climax. The total length at which this morphological transformation typically occurs is not rigidly fixed, but reproductive maturity is consistently attained at a modest body size. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies have established that puberty in Bay anchovy is reached at a total length of 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm], a value that corresponds closely with the size at which vitellogenesis is first detectable in females and spermiation begins in males. Reaching this size requires approximately two to three months of sustained feeding in productive estuarine environments, after which the fish are capable of participating in the spawning population during the same summer in which they were hatched, assuming favourable conditions prevail.

Once individuals have attained sexual maturity, the timing and magnitude of reproductive effort are strongly influenced by water temperature. The species is an iteroparous broadcast spawner, and a single gravid female can release multiple clutches of pelagic eggs over the course of the spawning season. At a sustained temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded reproductive output involves females releasing approximately 45110 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 45110 eggs per spawning event] and spawning daily [F_R_i = spawning daily], reflecting the combined effect of large clutch sizes and a short interval between successive spawnings. The energetic cost of such sustained gamete production is considerable, and females must maintain high ingestion rates to meet the basal maintenance requirements of daily tissue upkeep while simultaneously diverting resources toward vitellogenesis. Field collections of reproductively active females during summer peaks confirm that this high output is sustained only when prey densities are sufficient and water temperatures remain within the species' thermal optimum.

Body mass changes dramatically across the life cycle, from the negligible weight of the newly hatched prolarva to the substantially larger dimensions of the fully grown adult. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic mass of a fully grown individual that has completed its somatic growth, has been estimated from length-weight relationships derived from extensive field sampling. The maximum adult body mass attained by Bay anchovy is approximately 7.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.6 grams], a modest value consistent with the species' status as a small forage fish. In comparison, the wet weight at puberty, calculated from the same length-weight allometry at the size of 4 cm total length, is roughly 0.42 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.42 grams]. This nearly twenty-fold increase in mass from puberty to the ultimate adult size indicates that a considerable portion of somatic growth occurs after the onset of reproductive capability. Individuals that have just reached maturity are therefore relatively small and must allocate significant energetic resources toward continued increases in body length and mass, even as they begin to invest in gamete production. The trade-off between somatic growth and reproductive allocation is a central feature of the species' life history, particularly in environments where growing season length and prey availability are limiting.

Longevity in Bay anchovy is constrained by high natural mortality rates and the energetic demands of reproduction, and the species is short-lived compared to many other teleosts. Mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation indicate that the oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though most fish in wild populations likely survive for only one or two spawning seasons. The ultimate total length corresponding to this advanced age is about 10 cm [Li = about 10 cm], a size that is rarely observed in field collections because the vast majority of individuals succumb to predation or senescence before reaching this asymptotic length. The species exhibits an opportunistic, r-selected life history strategy that capitalises on ephemeral estuarine productivity. In this respect, Bay anchovy is typical of many small engraulids that serve as critical trophic links between zooplankton and larger piscivorous predators.
